meta.label: EN-A to low-end EN-B
meta.pilot_facing_title: Moving from an A wing to a low-B
meta.intro: 28 quick questions, one tap each. Answer honestly rather than optimistically — a "not yet" here is a useful, normal answer, and it tells you exactly what to work on next.
design_notes: No question asks which national pilot rating the pilot holds. Per knowledge/disagreements.md point 5, we ask about hours, flights, skills and conditions directly, because the national rating ladders don't map onto each other or onto EN A-D, and most users of a global web app won't hold one.
Hours are asked in broad bands, and cumulative hours are asked separately from recent hours, per knowledge/disagreements.md point 2.
Ground handling is asked about even though no numeric bar exists for it beyond Jerome Daoust's beginner checklist, per knowledge/disagreements.md point 11. It is weighted but never gated.
Ambitions are asked but carry no score of their own, per knowledge/disagreements.md point 9. They only matter in combination with thin readiness elsewhere.

The manoeuvre-course question is optional and can only ever add a small bonus, never subtract, per knowledge/disagreements.md point 1 and the brief. knowledge/steps/a-to-low-b.md notes no source treats SIV as relevant at this step at all, so it is not part of the scored set.

Several questions are deliberately not an ordered best-to-worst ladder (speed bar use, incidents, what happens in rough air, conditions flown). These are marked "ordered": false so the UI never implies the last option is the best one.

sections.title: On the ground and on launch

questions.text: Roughly how many hours have you flown in total, since you started?
questions.help: A rough band is fine. Count solo airtime, not tandems.

options.label: Under 10 hours
Between 10 and 25 hours
Between 25 and 50 hours
Between 50 and 100 hours
More than 100 hours

questions.text: Roughly how many flights have you done in total?
questions.help: Short top-to-bottoms and sledders all count.

options.label: Fewer than 15
Between 15 and 35
Between 35 and 75
More than 75

questions.text: And roughly how many hours have you flown in the last 12 months?
questions.help: We ask this separately on purpose — recent flying matters as much as your lifetime total.

options.label: Under 2 hours
Between 2 and 10 hours
Between 10 and 25 hours
More than 25 hours

questions.text: How much have you flown the wing you're on now?

options.label: I don't own one yet — I've been flying school or borrowed wings
Under 10 hours
Between 10 and 25 hours
Between 25 and 50 hours
More than 50 hours

questions.text: Where are you with your training?

options.label: Still in training, or still flying under instructor supervision
Just finished my course and cleared to fly on my own
Qualified a while ago and flying independently

questions.text: Over the last three months, how often have you actually got in the air?
questions.help: Think about months with flyable weather, not the whole calendar.

options.label: I haven't flown at all in the last three months
Less than once a month
About once a month
Two or three times a month
About once a week or more

questions.text: On a breezy day, how well can you hold the wing up facing it (reverse) and keep it there?

options.label: I haven't really tried this
It usually gets away from me within a few seconds
I can hold it for about ten seconds before I lose it
I can hold it steady for a minute or more
Steady, and I can walk around under it, turn it and manage stronger wind

questions.text: How often do you practise with the wing on the ground, away from flying?

options.label: Never — I only handle the wing when I'm about to fly
Once or twice ever
Now and then, when a day's unflyable
Regularly, as its own thing

questions.text: How often do your launches go cleanly, first attempt?
questions.help: Count both forward and reverse launches.

options.label: Not often — I regularly need several goes, get pulled around, or abort
About half the time
Most of the time — roughly three out of four
Nearly always, in the conditions I choose to fly

questions.text: Can you change speed while holding a straight line, and fly smooth turns both ways?
questions.help: Slowing towards minimum sink and speeding up again, without the wing wandering off heading; and tidy, coordinated 360s left and right.

options.label: Not confident with either yet
One of them, but not the other
Both, in calm air
Both, including in light thermals

questions.text: How close to a chosen spot do you normally land?

options.label: My approaches are still a bit hit and miss
I land safely, but not near a particular spot
Usually within a few wing-lengths of where I meant to
Consistently on the spot, flight after flight

questions.text: When the air gets bumpy, what do your hands actually do?

options.label: They stop moving — I hold still and wait it out
I grip the brakes and pull them in a bit
I try to react, but it's not automatic yet
I work the brakes to keep the pressure even and the wing overhead
That's automatic now — I'm feeling and correcting without thinking about it

questions.text: What kind of air have you been flying in, mostly?

options.label: Smooth evenings and calm mornings only
Light thermals and gentle ridge or coastal soaring
Moderate thermals, with some proper bumps in them
Strong thermic or mountain days fairly regularly

questions.text: How well can you see rough air coming before you're in it?
questions.help: Reading the forecast, the clouds, other pilots and the feel of the day, and getting down or staying away in good time.

options.label: Honestly, it usually catches me out — I find out when it's already rough
Sometimes I spot it, sometimes I don't
Usually, with enough time to land or move away
Yes — I plan my day around when it's likely to kick off
I only fly gentle conditions, so it hasn't really come up

questions.text: How do you use the speed bar at the moment?
questions.help: There's no wrong answer here — "never touched it" is completely normal on an A wing.

options.label: I've never used it
I've tried a little, gently, with plenty of height in smooth air
I use it to get out of sinking air, and otherwise leave it alone
I'm on bar fairly often when I'm gliding
I push a lot of bar, including fairly low down, to get back

questions.text: Have you had the wing collapse on you in flight, and what happened?
questions.help: A wing collapses so rarely on an A that "never" is a completely normal answer at this stage.

options.label: Never
Small tip collapses — the wing sorted itself out
Something bigger, and I caught it and flew it out
Yes, and I froze — the wing recovered on its own, not because of me
Yes, and it got away from me — I lost control of where the wing was going

questions.text: Can you pull big ears and get rid of them again when you need to come down?

options.label: I've never tried
Once or twice, with an instructor talking me through it
Yes, I'm comfortable with them
Yes, and I've got another way down as well if I need it

questions.text: Your reserve — where is it, and have you ever practised the throw?

options.label: I'm not completely sure I could find the handle in a hurry
I know exactly where the handle is, but I've never practised
I've practised the throw at least once, hanging in a harness
Practised recently, and the repack is up to date

questions.text: Have you done a manoeuvres course (over water, with an instructor)?
questions.help: Optional, and genuinely not expected at this stage. It can only help your result here, never hurt it.

options.label: No
Not yet, but I've got one booked
Yes, one
Yes, more than one

questions.text: Has anyone who has actually watched you fly said anything about a B wing?

options.label: An instructor or coach has told me to wait
Nobody who knows what they're looking at has seen me fly lately
Flying mates reckon I'd be fine on one
An instructor or coach has said I'm ready for one

questions.text: What's the main reason you want to move up?
questions.help: Pick the one that's closest to the truth, not the one that sounds best.

options.label: My wing now feels like it's holding back flying I can already do
My instructor or coach suggested it
I want more glide and speed for longer flights
I need a new wing anyway, so I may as well go a step up
Most people I fly with are on B wings and I don't want to be the odd one out
I'm hoping a better wing will cope with conditions I currently find hard

questions.text: What do you expect to actually change when you're on a low-B?

options.label: A bit more speed and glide — mostly it'll feel fairly similar
More feedback through the brakes, which I'll need to learn to read
I'm not really sure — I haven't looked into the differences
Flying will feel less of a struggle than it does now
It'll handle rough air better than my current wing does

questions.text: A new wing means a spell of relearning the basics on it — ground handling, launches, how it talks to you. How does that sit with you?

options.label: Fine — I'd spend time on the ground with it before flying anything demanding
Fine — I'd keep to easy days and easy sites for a while
I'd rather just get on and fly it
I'd expect to be straight back to normal on it within a flight or two

questions.text: What do you want to be doing more of over the next year?
questions.help: Pick any that apply. Wanting more is fine — this just helps us tailor the suggestions.

options.label: More local flying and soaring
My first cross-country flights
Long cross-country flights
Hike and fly in the mountains
Competitions
Acro or wing-overs
Nothing in particular — just enjoying it

questions.text: When the air gets properly rough, what usually happens for you?
questions.help: Everyone's heart rate goes up. We're asking what you do next.

options.label: I lock up a bit — I hang on and wait for it to pass
I get tense, want to land straight away, and my flying gets scrappier
Heart rate goes up, but I carry on flying the wing
I stay fairly calm, keep flying actively, and have a way out if it builds
It doesn't really bother me

questions.text: In the last few months, have you walked away from a launch, or landed early, because the day wasn't what you wanted to handle?

options.label: More than once, and I was happy with the call
Once or twice
No — I generally launch and see how it goes
No — it hasn't come up

questions.text: Your friends are launching into a day you're unsure about. What usually happens?

options.label: I go too — I don't want to be the one left on the hill
I feel the pull, but I usually wait
I make my own call and I'm comfortable either way
Hasn't come up

questions.text: In the last 12 months, any incidents or near misses? A messy launch, a hard landing, a scare in the air?
questions.help: Nobody sees this but you. An honest answer makes the result worth having.

options.label: Nothing I'd call a near miss
One or two moments that made me think — and I know what I'd do differently
A few, and I'm not really sure what went wrong
Something that shook me up, and I've been uneasy flying since
An injury, or I threw my reserve
